name: Volume eating

lead: Volume eating means choosing foods that give lots of bulk for few calories, such as vegetables and fruit, to feel full while dieting.
It is discussed in fat-loss circles. Source material specific to it is limited.

paras: Low-energy-density foods supply fewer calories relative to volume, so a reduced-calorie diet built from them is described as beneficial for weight management.
No direct harms reported for the dieting strategy in the sources. The same term describes compulsive large-volume eating in psychiatric and bariatric papers.

lead: Volume eating is the practice of building meals around low-energy-density foods, such as vegetables and fruit, that supply a lot of food by weight or volume for relatively few calories, with the aim of feeling full while cutting calorie intake. [1]

In looksmaxxing it is discussed as a way to lose body fat. Public health sources note that because fruits and vegetables have few calories relative to volume, eating them as part of a reduced-calorie diet can be beneficial for weight management. [1] Sources on the practice are limited, and no studies found tested it for appearance outcomes.

paras: The approach emphasises foods with few calories per unit of volume. A US Centers for Disease Control report describes fruits and vegetables as low in energy density and associated with decreased risk of chronic disease. [1]

In bariatric surgery literature, volume eating refers to eating large quantities after surgery and is cited as a cause of insufficient weight loss or weight regain after sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass. [2][3] Recent psychiatric papers describe compulsive high-volume eating and a fullness-seeking phenotype that overlaps with binge eating disorder and food addiction. [4][5] These uses differ from the dieting strategy described here.

No studies found of volume eating as a looksmaxxing practice. A CDC report on adult fruit and vegetable consumption in 2005 states that eating them in a reduced-calorie diet can aid weight management, and bariatric studies describe volume eating as a pattern linked to regain. [1][2][3]
